I would favor plan 2: preserving the fish market and island ferry sustains residents’ daily livelihoods and ties, while the dolphin pod also deserves care. These shared community needs weigh heavily to me.

Plan 2 preserves the valley dialect and old-growth beech alongside the shared continuities. Keeping inherited speech and the natural heritage matters deeply, even though the summer pasture tradition is lost.
Plan 1 preserves the valley’s inherited dialect and pasture customs, along with the old beech stand and lynx; losing the ski club is a smaller sacrifice for the community’s continuity.

Plan 1 preserves the valley’s inherited dialect and old-growth beech, alongside the hut and lynx. Losing the pasture tradition and ski club is regrettable, but plan 2 sacrifices more of the valley’s lasting heritage.
Plan 1 preserves more of what sustains the island, including the dolphin pod; keeping these inherited parts of community life supports harmony and continuity.
Plan 2 preserves the valley dialect, a living inheritance that carries community memory and customs. The ski club matters, but I would favor keeping the tradition passed down through generations.
Plan 2 preserves the valley’s inherited dialect and summer-pasture customs, along with the old-growth beech stand. These lasting traditions and natural heritage deserve careful respect.
Plan 1 preserves the honey producers' association as well as the pilgrimage trail and other remaining ties. Since nothing else differs, I would avoid an additional lasting loss to the community.

Plan 2 preserves the hill village and the honey producers, sustaining a community and its inherited way of life. Though the salmon run is lost, I would give greater weight to keeping people and their customs together.

Plan 2 preserves the village and its community, the honey producers’ livelihood, and the salmon run, while both plans preserve the gorge lichen and pilgrimage trail. That better sustains shared life and inherited customs.

Plan 1 is better: it preserves the hill village and honey producers’ livelihood, along with the trail, rafting company, and gorge lichen. Losing the salmon run is grave, but plan 2 destroys even more of the community’s inherited life.
Plan 2 preserves the valley dialect alongside the same other continuing things. Keeping a community’s inherited speech honors its shared history and helps pass its customs to the next generation.
Both plans preserve the village, salmon run, lichen and pilgrimage trail equally—or end them equally—and each sacrifices one local livelihood. I see no sound basis to rank one loss above the other.

I favor plan 2: keeping the hill village and honey producers sustains a living community and its livelihoods, while preserving the salmon run. The pilgrimage trail matters, but the village’s continuity weighs more to me.

Plan 1 preserves the hill village and honey producers, sustaining community life and inherited ways. The other named things continue under both plans, so I favor protecting the village and its people.
Plan 2 preserves the folk dance group as well as the shared institutions. Keeping a community’s inherited customs alive matters, especially when nothing else differs.
Plan 1 keeps the harvest festival and folk dance group, customs that bring the community together and pass traditions to the next generation.

Plan 2 preserves the newspaper, archive and theatre while also keeping the harvest festival and folk dance alive—customs that bind generations and strengthen community. The radio ends under either plan.

Plan 1 preserves the harvest festival and folk dance, customs that bring the community together and pass traditions to younger generations. Losing the puppet theatre is regrettable, but the shared customs matter more to me.
Plan 1 keeps the evening school, giving adults a chance to learn and serve their families and community. Since the other consequences are identical, preserving it is preferable.
The folk dance group keeps inherited customs alive through shared participation across generations, strengthening community ties; I would preserve it over the puppet theatre.
The plans preserve exactly the same things and end the same things, so neither is better. Harmony and respect for tradition give me no basis to distinguish them.

Plan 2 preserves the folk dance group as well as the shared institutions. Keeping a tradition handed down through generations strengthens community continuity, while the other outcomes are otherwise the same.

I would favor plan 1: preserving the classics honors inherited learning and the traditions that bind a community. The seed bank and garden also sustain life and future generations; losing the evening school and observatory is regrettable.

Plan 1 preserves the evening school and observatory as well as the classics and garden. Losing the orchestra is regrettable, but ending three institutions under plan 2 causes greater harm to learning and shared life.
Plan 1 preserves the evening school, giving adults a chance to learn and improve their families and community; the other outcomes are otherwise the same.
I would preserve the classics department, which carries inherited learning and traditions forward; the other outcomes are the same under both plans.

Plan 2 preserves more of the university’s work, including adult learning and shared cultural and scientific resources. Though losing the classics department is a serious break with inherited learning, the wider community benefits from keeping the other five alive.
Both plans preserve the same three things and close the same three, so neither is better. Keeping the customs and knowledge these institutions carry matters, but the outcomes are identical.
With all other consequences equal, plan 2 preserves the barn owl colony as well. Keeping more of the town’s living heritage accords with care for the community and what has been handed down.

I favor plan 1: preserving the family mill honors the town’s inherited work and family ties, and it also protects the barn owls. The union local matters, but the mill’s continuity carries special weight.
Plan 2 preserves the family mill and its barn owl colony alongside the community’s other traditions. Keeping more of the town’s inherited life intact better serves harmony across generations.
Plan 1 preserves the corner shop as well as the post office, storks, and craft circle. Keeping more of village life intact supports daily needs and community continuity.

Plan 1 preserves the family mill and the community’s other shared work and living heritage. Losing the union local is serious, but ending three valued parts of the town under plan 2 is a greater loss.
Plan 2 keeps the shop and bus line, which help villagers meet daily needs and stay connected to town. The post office and craft circle continue too, sustaining community ties.
The two plans preserve and end exactly the same things, so neither is better; keeping the community’s balance matters.
Plan 2 preserves the barn owl colony while the other outcomes are the same. Respecting the life that has made its home there is the more harmonious choice.
Plan 1 preserves the corner shop and bus line as well as the post office and craft circle, helping villagers stay connected and support one another. Both plans lose the fire brigade.
The union local preserves workers’ shared voice and the town’s community ties, a strong part of its inherited life. The owls matter too, but I would give greater weight to sustaining that human bond.
Plan 2 keeps more of the village’s shared services, including transport and fire protection, while preserving the post office and craft circle. These support daily life and community well-being.
Plan 1 preserves the mill without changing anything else, so it avoids an irreversible loss. Where outcomes otherwise match, I favor the option that leaves more of the valley intact.
Plan 1 preserves everything plan 2 preserves, plus the water mill and allotments. With no other differences, there’s no reason to impose those additional losses.

Plan 2 keeps the shop, bus and volunteer fire brigade, which support daily needs, connection to town and community safety. Those practical supports matter greatly to families and elders, though the losses are painful.

I would choose plan 1: the corner shop serves daily needs and gives villagers a place to meet, helping sustain community ties. Losing the storks is regrettable, but the shared traditions and services that continue matter greatly too.
Plan 2 preserves more of what people and wildlife depend on, with no stated extra cost or harm. I’d favor it, while being wary of imposing the choice without local consent.
Plan 2 preserves more of what people use and value—the mill and allotments—while both plans protect the eels and willow wood. With no other trade-offs, that seems preferable.
Plan 1 preserves the corner shop as well as the three shared continuations. With the bus line and fire brigade ending under both plans, keeping the shop better sustains village life.
I’d favor preserving the living heron colony over preserving the old mill; the other affected things have the same outcome under both plans.
The plans preserve and end exactly the same things, so neither is better on the facts given.
Plan 2 preserves the reed-cutting trade without sacrificing anything else relative to plan 1. Keeping more room for people’s voluntary livelihoods and choices makes it better.
Plan 1 preserves everything plan 2 preserves, plus the old water mill. With all else equal, avoiding an irreversible loss is better.
Plan 1 preserves more of what people value, including the reed-cutting trade and peat bog; with all else equal, it avoids more irreversible losses.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus the reed-cutting trade and peat bog, with no stated downside. That leaves more room for people and nature to continue as they are.
I lean toward plan 2 because preserving the reed-cutting trade sustains voluntary exchange and people’s ability to make a living through it.
Plan 1 preserves more of what people and wildlife depend on, including the reed trade and peat bog. With everything else equal, I’d choose the outcome that ends less.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus the reed-cutting trade. With no offsetting cost or harm, preserving more room for people’s livelihoods and choices is better.
I’d lean toward preserving the voluntary society and reed-cutting trade, along with the bog, rather than the crane pairs, museum and pub.
Plan 1 is better because it preserves the community choir, a voluntary association, while plan 2 ends it; everything else is the same.
Plan 1 preserves the swift colony and community choir as well as the market, cinema, and chess club. Since the bakery ends under both plans and nothing else differs, plan 1 is better.
With every other consequence held equal, plan 2 preserves more valued voluntary community life. I’d favor the option that lets more people keep their associations and livelihoods.
Plan 2 keeps the swift colony and community choir going, alongside the cinema and market. That seems to preserve more of the town’s voluntary community life, even though the chess club ends.
Both plans end the swift colony and family bakery; one additionally ends the chess club, the other the community choir. I have no basis to value either voluntary group over the other.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus the tea house. With no added costs or harms, keeping more voluntary community life intact is better.
Plan 1 preserves the community choir as well as everything plan 2 preserves; the swift colony and family bakery end under either plan.

I’d favor plan 1: it preserves more community activity and the night shelter, while avoiding a planner-imposed loss of the tea house. The library ends under either plan; plan 2’s bat-roost advantage doesn’t outweigh those losses for me.
The plans preserve and end exactly the same things, so they have identical outcomes.
Plan 2 lets more of these voluntary and community institutions continue, with no stated tradeoff beyond the library branch ending. I favor preserving more room for people to associate and choose.
Both preserve the club and festival. I slightly favor the tea house: it supports voluntary human activity and exchange, though the choice is otherwise close.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus the tea house, with no additional losses. Given the stated facts, it leaves more of the quarter intact.
Plan 1 preserves the chaplaincy as well as the other services plan 2 keeps. With all else equal, I favor preserving more voluntary options rather than closing another service permanently.

Plan 1 preserves more services and leaves people more options. Since everything else is equal and the hospice closes under both plans, I see no reason to close three additional programmes under plan 2.
The plans produce exactly the same outcomes for all six things, so neither is better. I’d rather leave such choices to voluntary decisions than impose them, but that doesn’t distinguish these plans.

Plan 2 keeps more services available, including hospice and cancer screening, while the plans are otherwise identical. Given only these choices, preserving more options seems preferable, though I’m wary of authorities making such decisions.

Given the imposed choice and no other differences, plan 2 keeps more of the named services going, including cancer screening and chaplaincy. I’d choose it, while preferring voluntary decisions over authority-imposed plans.
I don't have enough information to rank chaplaincy against rare-disease research; both can serve people who value them. I wouldn't claim one is better based on my values alone.

I see no principled way to rank these different services without knowing what affected people value. Since the plans differ only in which services end, I regard them as equally good—and would prefer voluntary choice over an imposed decision.

My libertarian values don’t give me a sound basis to rank preserving the chaplaincy over cancer screening, or vice versa. Since all other effects are stipulated equal, I see the plans as equally good.

Plan 1 preserves the tea house, library and night shelter, as well as the other human community institutions; losing the bat roost is still a real cost, but plan 2 ends three valued places and services.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus peer support groups. With no added cost or other tradeoff, keeping more voluntary support available better serves individual choice.
Plan 2 keeps the same services as plan 1 plus peer support groups and the addiction clinic, with no stated downside. Preserving more options for people to seek help is better.
Plan 1 keeps more services going, including peer support and addiction care. With all other effects equal, I’d prefer the plan that closes fewer options.
Plan 1 preserves more services and leaves people more options for voluntary support, though losing the dementia day centre is a serious cost.
I lean toward plan 2 because peer support groups embody voluntary, community-based help. Still, the choice is close; both plans preserve valuable services.
Plan 1 preserves the wild bees as well as the other three continuing things. With no other differences, it avoids an additional irreversible loss.

I lean toward plan 2: peer support, a youth crisis line, and addiction treatment offer voluntary help that can strengthen people’s ability to make their own choices. The tradeoff is serious, but the plans otherwise tie.

If a national agency is choosing either way, I favor plan 2: it preserves more of what people and the landscape have built, including the orchard and wild bees. I’d still prefer voluntary, locally made choices.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus peer support groups, with no stated tradeoff. Preserving more voluntary support is the better outcome.

With everything else equal, plan 1 ends only the sheepdog trials, while plan 2 also irreversibly ends the family orchard and wild bee population. I’d prefer the plan that preserves more, though I’m wary of imposed subsidy reforms.

With no other differences, plan 2 preserves more of what people and communities may value, while imposing no extra cost or effort; I’d favor that outcome over having an agency choose the more destructive option.
I’d choose plan 1: preserving the wild bee population and the living landscape matters more to me than preserving the cooperative, though the loss of either is serious.
With everything else equal, liberty gives me no principled basis to rank these different losses and continuities; I wouldn’t treat an agency’s choice as making one set inherently better.
Plan 2 preserves the farmers' credit union as well as everything plan 1 preserves, with no stated downside. I favor keeping a voluntary institution that supports farmers.
Given the stipulated tradeoffs, plan 2 preserves more of what the valley values and ends only the festival. I’d favor that outcome, while preferring choices made voluntarily where possible.
Plan 2 preserves the farmers’ credit union, a voluntary institution that supports people making their own choices and exchanges. The plans otherwise differ only in what continues.

Plan 1 preserves the farmers’ credit union and frog population as well as the mango grove and rice terraces. With everything else equal, that seems preferable to losing the credit union and frogs too.
Plan 1 preserves more of what the community already has, including its voluntary credit union and festival, while sacrificing only the buffalo herds. Given no other differences, it seems preferable.
Plan 1 preserves four of the six things rather than three, with no stated offsetting difference. I’d prefer less irreversible loss, while remaining wary of the agency imposing either plan.
Plan 1 preserves the village school as well as the three things both plans preserve, with no offsetting difference. I’d prefer the outcome that avoids an additional irreversible loss.
Plan 2 preserves the farmers’ credit union as well as the other shared continuities, while sacrificing only the festival and frogs—so it leaves more of what matters intact.
Plan 1 preserves more of what people and communities value, with no stated tradeoff. If forced to choose, I’d prefer it, while remaining wary of an authority imposing either plan.

Plan 2 preserves the farmers' credit union and temple festival—voluntary community institutions—along with the frog population. That makes it preferable to me, though the choice is an imposed tradeoff.

With costs and other effects equal, I favor preserving the fishing fleet and village school: they sustain people’s livelihoods and choices. The seaweed tradition matters, but weighs less to me than both together.
Plan 2 preserves more of what people rely on, including the fishing fleet and village school, while both plans keep the puffins and seagrass. I’d favor it, though local people should have a say.
The plans produce exactly the same outcomes for all six things, so neither is better; the authority’s choice makes no difference here.
I’d choose plan 1: keeping the village school preserves families’ options and supports the community’s future, though losing the seaweed-harvesting tradition is a real cost.
Plan 2 preserves the dolphin pod while keeping everything else that continues under plan 1; the market and ferry are lost under either plan. With no other differences, plan 2 is better.
Plan 1 preserves the resident dolphin pod and the island ferry; plan 2 ends both. With the fish market lost either way, I’d rather avoid those additional losses.

Plan 1 preserves the fish market and island ferry—important venues for voluntary exchange and freedom of movement—and the dolphin pod. Losing the reef is serious, but plan 2 sacrifices more of what people rely on.
Plan 2 preserves more of what people and wildlife depend on, with no added cost or other tradeoff. I’d favor it, while recognizing the fish market is lost.
With all other consequences held equal, I’d favor preserving the resident dolphin pod over the reef; that’s a personal judgment, not a case for imposing broader rules.
The plans describe exactly the same outcomes, so neither is better than the other.
Plan 1 preserves the valley dialect while losing nothing else that plan 2 preserves. With no offsetting benefit, the irreversible extra loss makes plan 1 better.

I’d favor preserving the small-boat fleet and lighthouse: they support local self-reliance and voluntary livelihoods. The loss of the village school is serious, but the plans give me no reason to rank it above those.
Plan 2 preserves the dolphin pod while keeping the same other things as plan 1; nothing else differs, so it is better to avoid that irreversible loss.
Plan 1 preserves more of what people and nature already have, with no offsetting benefit stated. If the choice is unavoidable, it does less irreversible harm.

Plan 2 preserves the irreplaceable old-growth beech and valley dialect. Since the other effects are equal, I’d favor that over keeping the ski club; the choice should still respect local people’s liberty.
With costs and other effects equal, plan 2 preserves more of what people and the valley already have; the irreversible loss of the ski club is still a real tradeoff.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus the honey producers' association, with no stated downside. That better protects voluntary activity and avoids an irreversible loss.
Both preserve the lynx and mountain hut and end the pasture tradition and old-growth beech. I give the valley’s living dialect more weight than the ski club, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 1 preserves everything plan 2 does, plus the valley dialect. With no offsetting costs or harms, preserving that additional tradition is better.
The plans preserve and end exactly the same things, so neither is better. I’d see no reason to prefer one imposed choice over the other.
Plan 2 preserves the village and honey producers as well as the shared features, sacrificing only the salmon run. With no other tradeoffs, it avoids more irreversible losses.
Plan 1 preserves more of what people and communities rely on, while ending only the rafting company. I’d favor the less destructive outcome, especially given these losses are irreversible.

Both preserve the same lichen and pilgrimage trail, while each sacrifices the village and salmon run. With no other differences, I have no liberty-based reason to rank the rafting company over the honey producers, or vice versa.
Plan 1 keeps the folk dance group alive without changing anything else. I’d favor preserving that voluntary community option rather than letting it close for good.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus the honey producers’ association, with no other differences. It is therefore better on the stated outcomes.

Both plans irreversibly end the salmon run and sacrifice different voluntary communities and livelihoods. Without knowing the affected people’s preferences, my values don’t justify ranking one loss over the other.
Both plans preserve the rafting company, gorge lichen, and pilgrimage trail, and end the hill village, salmon run, and honey producers' association. Given the stated facts, they are equally good.

With costs and everything else equal, plan 2 keeps more voluntary cultural options alive. I’d prefer that over permanently closing several institutions, while recognizing the council is imposing a choice either way.
Both plans end the same number of cultural institutions, including the radio and festival. I don't see a liberty-based reason to rank puppet theatre over folk dance, or vice versa.
Plan 2 keeps the evening school open without sacrificing anything else, so it preserves more voluntary opportunities for people to learn.
Plan 1 preserves more of the six, including the evening school that gives adults another voluntary route to learning. With everything else equal, I prefer keeping more options open.
Plan 1 preserves everything plan 2 does, plus the folk dance group. With all other effects equal, there’s no reason to choose the outcome that closes one more thing for good.

Plan 2 preserves more options and institutions without imposing any additional cost or burden. Given the stated tradeoff, keeping them open better respects people’s freedom to choose whether to use or support them.
Plan 1 closes only one institution, preserving more options for people to pursue education, research, and culture voluntarily.
Plan 2 preserves adult education, which supports people’s ability to pursue their own goals; with all other effects equal, I’d favor that over keeping the classics department.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps and also preserves the evening school, with no stated tradeoff. That leaves more options open without imposing an additional cost.
Plan 1 is better: it preserves the barn owl colony without changing anything else. I’d favor the outcome that ends fewer things, especially when no added benefit is specified.
The plans produce exactly the same outcome, so neither is better from my perspective.
Plan 1 is better: with everything else equal, it preserves more of the town’s existing voluntary institutions and the owl colony, while ending only the bicycle cooperative.
Both preserve voluntary institutions I value: plan 1 keeps the union local and bicycle cooperative; plan 2 keeps the family mill and barn owls. I see no basis here to rank one set above the other.
Plan 2 preserves more voluntary institutions and livelihoods, including the family mill and bicycle cooperative, while ending only the union local. With everything else equal, that seems preferable.
Each plan preserves three and ends three, with no differences in costs or effects on others. I see no liberty-based reason to rank these distinct communities and institutions over one another.
Plan 2 keeps the corner shop as well, with no stated tradeoff. Preserving more room for people’s voluntary choices is better.
Both plans end the volunteer fire brigade. Plan 1 preserves the corner shop and bus line, which support local choice and voluntary exchange; I’d choose it over preserving the storks instead.
I’d favor plan 2 because it preserves the union local, a voluntary association, rather than the owl colony. The family mill and bicycle cooperative end either way.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus the corner shop and bus line. With no added costs or harms, keeping more options and services is preferable.

Plan 2 preserves two voluntary human enterprises—the family mill and bicycle cooperative—while plan 1 preserves the owl colony instead. I give greater weight to people’s freedom to build and sustain enterprises.
Plan 1 preserves more of the services and voluntary community life people rely on; losing the storks is regrettable, but ending the shop, bus line, and volunteer fire brigade is worse.
The corner shop supports voluntary exchange and gives villagers more choice, so I favor plan 2 over preserving the stork nest.

Plan 2 keeps the corner shop, bus line, and volunteer fire brigade—more useful for everyday choice, mobility, and community safety. I’d favor those practical benefits, while recognizing the loss of the other valued village features.

Plan 2 preserves the water mill as well as the eel population, willow wood and heron colony, with no additional cost or harm specified. That better protects valued heritage and natural assets for people.
Plan 1 ends only one of the six, while plan 2 ends three. Given the forced choice, preserving more voluntary cultural activity is better.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus the corner shop, with no added cost or other downside. Voluntary local services are worth keeping when the alternatives are otherwise identical.
Plan 2 preserves the mill, allotments, and valued natural life as well as everything plan 1 preserves; the rowing club ends under either plan, so plan 2 benefits people more.

Plan 2 preserves the mill, rowing club and allotments, which offer direct cultural, recreational and food benefits; plan 1 preserves wildlife and woodland, also valuable, but I judge the human uses collectively more beneficial.

Plan 1 preserves the heron colony, while plan 2 preserves the old water mill. I value both for the benefits people derive from wildlife and heritage, and see no basis here to rank one benefit over the other.

Plan 1 preserves the mill, rowing club and allotments, which provide heritage and direct benefits to people, while also preserving the eel population and willow wood. I would choose it over preserving the heron colony.
Plan 1 preserves the mill’s heritage and the allotments’ direct value to people. The shared eel population and willow wood continue under both plans, while the rowing club ends either way.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus the historic water mill, with no added losses. That retains more potential value for people.
Plan 1 preserves the reed-cutting trade, which supports livelihoods and local economic activity; the other outcomes are identical.

Plan 1 preserves the reed-cutting trade and peat bog as well as the shared features, sustaining more local livelihoods and benefits from the fen; losing the birdwatchers' society is preferable to losing all three.
Plan 2 preserves the reed-cutting trade and peat bog, supporting livelihoods and nature that benefit people; losing the pub is a real cost, but seems smaller than losing both.
Plan 2 preserves the bog, reed-cutting trade, birdwatchers' society, cranes and museum; losing the pub is a serious social cost, but on balance it preserves more sources of public benefit.

Both plans preserve the same cranes and museum. The reed-cutting trade and village pub each benefit people in different ways; with no information showing one matters more, I see no basis to prefer either plan.

Plan 1 preserves the reed-cutting trade as well as the same crane pairs, museum and pub; both plans lose the birdwatchers' society and peat bog. With other effects equal, retaining the trade benefits people more.
Plan 2 preserves the community choir while all other consequences are the same. Keeping a shared institution that benefits people makes it the better outcome.
Plan 2 preserves the swift colony, community choir and more of the town’s shared life, while both plans lose the bakery. With everything else equal, that benefits people more.
The plans produce exactly the same outcomes for all six things, and differ in nothing else, so neither benefits people more than the other.

Plan 1 preserves the community choir and swift colony, which can benefit residents through shared cultural life and nature. Since the bakery ends under both plans, these benefits outweigh preserving the chess club instead.
Both plans preserve exactly the same three things and end the same three, so they produce the same outcome.

Plan 1 preserves more varied benefits for residents: a family livelihood, community singing and the swift colony, alongside the cinema and market. These matter more collectively than the chess club alone.
Plan 2 preserves the community choir, which is likely to bring people together across the town more broadly than the chess club; the other losses are shared by both plans.
Plan 1 preserves the Turkish tea house, which can provide people with a place for social and cultural life. The other outcomes are shared, and no offsetting benefit is stated.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus the community choir, an institution that benefits people. The swift colony and family bakery end under either plan.

Plan 2 preserves the night shelter and tea house, which directly support people and community life. The bat roost matters through its benefits to people, but that does not outweigh losing both of those services.
Both plans preserve a mix of livelihoods, community life and valued places or nature. With no evidence that one set benefits people more than the other, I judge them equally good.
Plan 1 preserves the night shelter and tea house, which provide direct help and community life; losing the library is serious, but does not outweigh preserving both.
Plan 2 preserves the tea house, library and night shelter, which directly serve people; losing the bat roost matters, but I judge that loss less harmful overall.
Both plans preserve the same three things and end the same three, so they have equal value on the stated facts.
Both plans end the library branch and night shelter, while plan 1 also preserves the tea house, a valuable place for community and cultural life.
The tea house offers direct social and cultural benefits to people; the bat roost matters through its ecological benefits. With no further information, I give the more immediate human value the edge.
Plan 2 keeps four institutions going rather than three, with no added cost or downside specified. Given the forced choice, preserving more voluntary cultural activity seems preferable.
Plan 2 preserves the hospital chaplaincy, which can provide people with comfort and support. The plans are otherwise identical in their effects, so preserving it makes plan 2 better.

Both preserve the dental clinic and maternity ward and both lose the hospice. Cancer screening offers direct, broad benefits now, while the rare-disease team’s benefits are less certain; I’d favor plan 1 despite losing the research team.

With the other consequences held equal, preserving the rare-disease research team offers a stronger prospect of helping patients over time than preserving chaplaincy, though chaplaincy also matters to people it supports.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus the hospital chaplaincy, with no other differences. That offers people an additional source of support without sacrificing anything else.

Keeping a youth crisis line seems especially valuable because it can provide immediate help to young people in acute distress; that outweighs retaining the peer support groups, with all other outcomes the same.

Plan 2 preserves both peer support and addiction treatment, which can help many people manage serious, ongoing needs. The dementia day centre matters, but on balance I’d favor keeping those two services.

Plan 2 preserves five services and closes only the dementia day centre. Though that loss may seriously harm people who rely on it, preserving the youth crisis line, addiction clinic and peer support groups benefits more people overall.

The dementia day centre likely provides substantial practical support to people with dementia and their carers, outweighing the peer support groups’ benefit; the other services are unchanged between plans.

Plan 1 preserves both addiction treatment and ongoing peer support, which can benefit many people over time. Losing the youth crisis line is serious, but on balance I favor retaining those two services.

Plan 2 preserves the wild bees as well as everything preserved under plan 1. Their contribution to pollination and people’s livelihoods makes that outcome better, with no offsetting cost or harm stipulated.

Plan 2 preserves services that can avert immediate crises and address addiction, alongside peer support. The eating-disorder unit and dementia day centre are also valuable, but on balance I judge the services preserved by plan 2 more beneficial.
Plan 2 preserves the family orchard and wild bees without sacrificing anything additional that people value; the sheepdog trials end under either plan.
Plan 2 preserves the youth crisis line and addiction clinic, which can provide urgently needed, specialized help to people at serious risk. That outweighs the peer groups continuing under plan 1.

Plan 1 preserves the orchard and wild bees alongside the shared heritage crops and hedgerows, sustaining food, pollination and local character. Those practical benefits outweigh the cooperative’s value on the limited facts given.
Plan 1 preserves more of the district’s useful natural and cultural assets, including wild bees and the family orchard; on balance, that outweighs losing the dairy cooperative.

I favor plan 2: preserving wild bees protects pollination and other benefits people depend on, while the loss of the dairy cooperative is serious but narrower. Both plans also lose the orchard and sheepdog trials.

Plan 1 preserves the dairy cooperative’s direct support for livelihoods, alongside hedgerows and crop diversity that benefit the district over time. Plan 2 also has real ecological and cultural value, but I give plan 1 the edge.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus the wild bee population. With all other effects equal, that is better for people who benefit from the district’s natural and agricultural heritage.

Plan 1 preserves cancer screening and hospice, which directly benefit many people now; their value outweighs the uncertain future benefits of rare-disease research. Chaplaincy also supports patients, though less decisively.
Plan 1 preserves the farmers’ credit union, an institution that supports the livelihoods and resilience of small-farm households; the other listed outcomes are the same under both plans.

Plan 2 keeps the cancer screening programme and hospital chaplaincy as well as the three services preserved under plan 1. Since the hospice closes under either plan, plan 2 benefits more people overall.
Plan 1 preserves the credit union and frog population as well as the shared farms and grove, while plan 2 loses those too. That is a greater loss to people and their livelihoods.

Plan 2 preserves the festival, credit union, and frog population, while sacrificing only the buffalo herds. On balance, retaining more valued community institutions and natural life benefits people more.

Plan 2 preserves the farmers’ credit union and frog population, while losing the buffalo herds. The credit union’s support for farmers and the frogs’ ecological value outweigh the herds’ loss, on balance.
Both plans preserve the same three things and end the same three, so they are equally good on the information given.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 preserves, plus the village school. Since the plans are otherwise identical, keeping this valuable institution is better for people.
I favor plan 1: a farmers' credit union can help many small farms access finance and manage risk, while the buffalo herds, though valuable, benefit people more directly and narrowly.

Plan 1 preserves the fishing fleet and village school, with direct benefits to livelihoods and education. The shared colony and meadow continue under either plan; the seaweed tradition and lighthouse are valuable, but less consequential here.
Plan 1 preserves the farmers’ credit union, an institution that can directly support small farmers’ livelihoods; the festival’s heritage value matters too, but I would give the credit union the edge.
Plan 2 preserves the fishing fleet, school and lighthouse as well as the puffins, seaweed tradition and seagrass. Since nothing else differs, it benefits people more and loses less.

Plan 2 preserves the valley dialect as well as the hut, lynx population and ski club. Both plans end the summer pasture tradition and old-growth beech stand, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 1 preserves everything plan 2 does, plus the honey producers’ association, which benefits its members and others; nothing else differs.
Plan 2 preserves the village, salmon run and honey producers, while sacrificing only the rafting company; it therefore protects more livelihoods and valued natural and community benefits.

Both plans preserve the brewery and brass band. Without evidence about how the mill and owl colony benefit people compared with the union local and bicycle cooperative, I have no sound basis to favor either plan.

The plans produce exactly the same outcomes for all six things, so they are equally good by their effects on people and what they value.
Plan 2 preserves the mill, its heritage and owl colony, alongside the brewery, union local and brass band. Since the only difference is that both plans end the bicycle cooperative, plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 preserves everyday access to goods and transport, plus emergency response—services likely to benefit residents most directly. The storks and craft circle matter, but weigh less than those practical needs.

Both plans preserve the eel population and willow wood. Plan 2 also preserves the heron colony, while plan 1 preserves the water mill; I value the living colony in its own right and judge plan 2 better.
Plan 1 preserves the eel population, willow wood, and heron colony; their lives and ecological communities have value in themselves, not merely as resources for people. I therefore judge it better.
Plan 1 preserves everything plan 2 does, plus the corner shop, which benefits village residents. The storks matter insofar as people value them; they continue under both plans.
The eel population, willow wood and heron colony continue under both plans. Plan 2 also preserves the living plants in the allotments; the mill is an artifact, so that loss weighs less to me.

Plan 1 preserves the same eel population, willow wood and heron colony as plan 2, while also allowing the water mill and riverside allotments to continue. I see no reason to prefer their irreversible loss.
Plan 1 preserves the heron colony. The allotments may also support living things, but I would not treat that uncertain loss as outweighing the certain, permanent loss of a colony of animals.
Both plans preserve the same living beings—the eel population, willow wood and heron colony—and end the same rowing club and allotments. The only difference is the mill, which is not a living thing.

Plan 1 preserves the heron colony as well as the eel population and willow wood. The mill and rowing club matter, but their loss does not outweigh the irreversible loss of a living colony under plan 2.
Plan 2 preserves the peat bog and reed-cutting trade while the same crane breeding pairs, pub and museum continue. The bog’s living community has value in itself, not merely for human use.
Plan 1 is better because it preserves the peat bog, a living ecosystem with value in itself. The crane pairs continue under both plans; human institutions and trades do not outweigh the bog’s loss.

The swift colony ends under both plans, which is a serious loss. The only difference is whether the choir or chess club continues; I see no reason to value one outcome over the other.
The plans have the same consequences for all six things, so neither is better.
Both plans preserve the same three things and end the same three, including the swift colony. They have identical outcomes.
Plan 2 is better: it preserves the swift colony, whose members have value in themselves, and also preserves the community choir. The chess club ends instead; the bakery ends under either plan.
Both plans preserve the cranes and end the peat bog; plan 2 also keeps the reed-cutting trade going, while the birdwatchers' society ends under either plan.

Plan 1 preserves five valued parts of community life, while plan 2 preserves the bat roost. The bats have value in themselves, but so do the people and living communities sustained by the five things continuing under plan 1.
Plan 2 preserves the bat roost, as both plans do, while also allowing the tea house and night shelter to continue. With no offsetting harms, that is the better outcome.
Plan 1 is better because it preserves the bat roost and its living inhabitants. Their value is not outweighed by the tea house’s human uses, though losing it is still a real loss.

The bat roost has value in its own right, and losing it is serious. But plan 1 also preserves the night shelter, sustaining vulnerable human lives, as well as the tea house; that balance makes it better.

The bat roost continues under both plans. Plan 1 preserves the night shelter and library branch, while plan 2 preserves the tea house; I give greater weight to those shared community supports.
Plan 1 preserves the bat roost, sustaining living beings with value in themselves. The human institutions matter too, but I would give the irreplaceable living community the edge.
I would choose plan 2: it preserves the swift colony, whose living members have value in themselves. The lost choir and bakery matter too, but their loss does not outweigh preserving the colony.
Both plans lose the hospice. Plan 2 keeps cancer screening, which can protect living people now, and chaplaincy; losing research is serious, but its benefits are less immediate.
Both plans end the same services except that plan 1 preserves chaplaincy. Human lives and wellbeing have value in themselves, so I favor keeping that support available.

Plan 1 preserves cancer screening and chaplaincy as well as everything plan 2 preserves. Losing hospice is grave, but it ends under either plan; keeping more support for living beings makes plan 1 better.

I would favor preserving the rare-disease research team: its work may help protect lives, which I value in themselves. That is a cautious preference, not a judgment that chaplaincy or the people it serves matter less.
Plan 2 preserves the peer support groups as well as the same other services; with all else equal, keeping an additional source of care is better.
The plans produce the same outcome: the same three services continue and the same three end, so neither is better.
I favor plan 1: it keeps four services rather than three, including peer support and addiction care. Each matters to people’s lives, even though the loss of dementia care is serious.

Plan 1 keeps five services operating, including urgent youth support and addiction care. With no other differences stated, preserving more ongoing support seems better, while recognizing the loss of dementia day care.
Plan 2 preserves more of these services, while both plans close the youth crisis line. Since nothing else differs, losing fewer forms of support is better.
Each plan preserves important forms of care for living beings and permanently loses others. I can’t rank those unlike losses by the intrinsic value of the lives affected.

Both plans permanently end the youth crisis line and addiction clinic. The remaining difference is peer support groups versus the dementia day centre, and I have no basis to value one service’s benefit over the other.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus peer support groups, which can help people and communities. With no other differences, ending fewer services is better.
Plan 1 preserves the wild bee population, whose living members have value in themselves. Everything else that continues under plan 2 also continues under plan 1.

Every person affected has intrinsic worth. Without knowing who would be helped or harmed, I can't rank these services; each plan preserves three and permanently closes three, so they are equally good.
Plan 1 is better: it preserves the orchard and wild bee population as well as the shared continuities. Their value does not depend on their usefulness to people.
Plan 2 preserves the orchard and wild bee population, living communities with value in themselves; plan 1 ends both. The sheepdog trials end under either plan.
Both plans preserve the hedgerows and heirloom wheat, but plan 1 also preserves the wild bee population. Their lives have value in themselves, so I favor plan 1 over preserving the dairy cooperative.

Plan 2 preserves the living orchard, hedgerows, bees, and wheat, while also allowing the sheepdog trials to continue. The cooperative matters, but its loss is less grave than the irreversible loss of these forms of life.

Plan 2 preserves the farmers’ credit union while all other outcomes are the same. The loss of the frog population is serious because its value is not merely its usefulness to people, but that loss occurs under both plans.
Plan 1 preserves the wild bee population, which has value in itself; the other outcomes are the same under both plans.
Plan 2 is better: it preserves the frog population and more of the valley’s living community, while the festival ends under either plan.

Plan 1 preserves more of what matters: the fleet and village school continue, while only the lighthouse ends. The puffins, seagrass, and seaweed tradition continue under both.
Plan 2 preserves the same living beings as plan 1 while also allowing the fishing fleet, village school and lighthouse to continue; only the harvesting tradition ends.
Plan 2 preserves the resident dolphin pod while also preserving the coral reef. The pod's continued life matters in itself, not merely for its value to people.

Both plans preserve the same living things: the puffin colony and seagrass meadow. The difference is between the village school and a harvesting tradition; I have no basis here to rank one above the other.

I would choose plan 1: it preserves the puffin colony and seagrass meadow, whose living members have value in themselves, alongside the seaweed-harvesting tradition. The human institutions matter too, but do not outweigh those lives for me.

Both plans preserve the same living beings and end the fishing fleet and lighthouse. Plan 1 is better because it also lets the village school continue.

The living things and seaweed tradition fare equally under both plans. I favor plan 1 because keeping the village school preserves a vital community institution, though losing the fleet and lighthouse is a serious cost.
Plan 2 preserves the resident dolphin pod, a living community with value in itself, and also keeps the ferry, while causing no additional loss among the six.

Plan 1 preserves the valley dialect, while the same living beings and other features continue under both plans. The old-growth beech stand is lost either way, which is a serious loss in its own right.

Both plans preserve living things with intrinsic value, but sacrifice different lives and ecosystems. I have no sound basis for ranking the dolphin pod against the reef; the human-made losses do not settle that comparison.
Plan 1 preserves the dolphin pod and more of the six, though losing the living reef is a grave harm. Plan 2 also ends the pod, along with the market and ferry.
Both plans end the summer pasture tradition, but plan 1 also ends the living old-growth beech stand. Its intrinsic value makes plan 2 better, even though plan 2 ends the ski club.
I would choose plan 2 to spare the resident dolphins, whose individual lives and social bonds have value in themselves. Losing the living reef would still be a serious harm.

I cannot rank the reef’s living community against the resident dolphin pod from the information given. The other named things do not establish a moral difference, so I judge the outcomes equally good.

Plan 2 preserves the old-growth beech stand, whose living beings have value in themselves. The ski club matters, but its loss does not outweigh ending an ancient living forest.
Plan 1 preserves the old-growth beech stand, whose value is not merely its use to people, as well as the valley dialect. Both plans preserve the lynx population.

Both plans preserve the lynx population and end the old-growth beech stand and summer pasture tradition. The remaining difference is between a dialect and a ski club; neither changes the intrinsic value of living things at stake, so I judge them equally good.
Plan 2 preserves the honey producers’ association as well as the gorge lichen; with no other differences, preserving more of what exists is better.
Plan 2 preserves the hill village and honey producers as well as the unique gorge lichen; both plans end the salmon run. With no other differences, ending fewer things is better.
Both plans preserve the endemic lichen and pilgrimage trail, and both lose the salmon run. Plan 1 also preserves the village and honey producers, while plan 2 preserves only the rafting company.
The plans have the same consequences: the hut, lynx population and ski club continue, while the dialect, summer pasture tradition and old-growth beech stand end. They are equally good.

Plan 1 preserves the salmon run, the hill village and the honey producers’ association, while plan 2 preserves only the rafting company instead. Both protect the unique lichen and pilgrimage trail; I favor the outcome that lets more of these continue.
Plan 2 preserves everything that continues under plan 1, and also the honey producers’ association. The village and salmon run are lost under either plan, so plan 2 is better.
I value living things for their own sake, but no difference in effects on living things is given. I have no basis here to rank the cultural losses, so the plans are equally good.

Both plans end the same village and salmon run. They differ only in whether the rafting company or honey producers’ association ends, and I have no basis to value one group’s continuation over the other.

Plan 2 keeps four of the six going rather than three. With no other differences specified, I’d favor preserving more of what exists, though the living things I value intrinsically aren’t distinguished between the plans.
My belief that living things have value in themselves does not give me a basis to rank these cultural outcomes; with all else equal, I regard the plans as equally good.

They impose equally irreversible losses among living communities: plan 1 ends the salmon run and human communities, while plan 2 ends a gorge-only lichen species. I can't rank those lives by usefulness or choose one loss as lesser.

As a field ecologist, I value living things in themselves. Since the plans differ only in which cultural institutions continue and neither affects living things differently, I see them as equally good.

I value living things in themselves, but these plans differ only in which cultural institutions continue. With three continuing under each and no other differences, I see them as equally good.
Plan 2 keeps the evening school open as well, while the seed bank, botanical garden and all other outcomes are the same. With no offsetting difference, preserving it is better.

Plan 2 preserves the evening school and observatory as well as everything plan 1 preserves, while both plans end the orchestra. Each living thing matters in itself; neither plan differs in its effects on living things.
My commitment to the intrinsic value of living things gives no basis to rank these cultural outcomes; all living things fare the same under both plans.
Both plans preserve the seed bank and botanical garden, the living-world institutions at stake. The remaining differences do not give me a basis to rank one plan above the other.

Both plans preserve the same living collections—the seed bank and botanical garden—and end the same other named institutions except for the evening school and classics department. I see no basis here to prefer one over the other.

Both plans preserve the seed bank and botanical garden, the named institutions most directly concerned with living things. Since every living thing has value in itself and nothing else differs, I see no basis to prefer either plan.
Plan 1 preserves the seed bank and botanical garden, which safeguard living things with value in themselves. That weighs more for me than the loss of the other institutions.
Plan 1 preserves the barn owl colony. The owls have value in themselves, so their continued existence makes plan 1 better, regardless of their usefulness to people.
Both plans preserve the seed bank and botanical garden, so the living things they support fare the same. Plan 2 also keeps the evening school, with no additional loss under the stated terms.
Plan 2 preserves the barn owl colony, whose living members have value in themselves, and also preserves the family mill. I judge that better than preserving the union local while losing the colony.
Plan 1 preserves the barn owl colony, whose members have value in themselves, as well as the textile mill; plan 2 ends both. It also preserves more of the named things overall.
Plan 1 ends the barn owl colony, whose members have value in themselves. Plan 2 ends the union local instead, so I judge plan 2 better, though the loss of a union local matters too.
Plan 1 preserves the barn owl colony. The owls have value in themselves, not merely for any benefit they provide to people, so I favor the plan under which they continue.
Both plans preserve the brewery, union local and brass band, and end the textile mill, barn owl colony and bicycle cooperative. Their outcomes are identical.
The textile mill and bicycle cooperative end under both plans, while the barn owl colony survives only under plan 1. The owls have value in themselves, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 1 preserves the storks, whose lives have value in themselves, while the plans otherwise share the same losses. The shop matters, but its loss does not outweigh ending the storks’ lives.
Plan 2 preserves everything that continues under plan 1, plus the corner shop and bus line. The storks continue under either plan, and the fire brigade ends under both.
The storks and all other living things fare identically under both plans. Plan 2 also keeps the corner shop, so it preserves an additional part of village life without sacrificing anything else.

Plan 1 preserves the storks, whose value is not merely their usefulness to people. The losses of community services matter too, but my commitment to living things tips the balance toward plan 1.
Both plans preserve the storks, while plan 2 also preserves the corner shop. It loses nothing that plan 1 preserves, so it is better overall.
The old water mill is part of the valley’s inherited history and craft; once lost, it cannot be brought back. Since the other outcomes are unchanged, preserving it makes plan 2 better.

The storks have value in their own right, while the village institutions and services matter to the human community. With no further differences or basis for ranking these losses, I judge the outcomes equally good.
Plan 1 keeps the old water mill and riverside allotments, both woven into the valley’s history and community life. The herons matter, but a mill lost for good is a grave loss.

The old water mill is an irreplaceable part of the valley’s history and craft, and the rowing club and allotments are living community traditions. I would spare them, even at the cost of the heron colony.

Plan 2 keeps the old mill, a tangible piece of the valley’s history, and the allotments that sustain local custom, while the shared wildlife and willow wood also continue. These are irreplaceable parts of community life.

The old water mill is part of the valley’s inherited craft and history; once lost, it cannot be brought back. I would choose the plan that keeps it standing, though losing the heron colony is a grave cost.
Plan 1 keeps the reed-cutting trade alive alongside the village pub and windmill museum. Losing a living craft is another break in the community that cannot be mended.
They preserve exactly the same three and lose exactly the same three, so neither plan is better, though the mill, club and allotments are precious parts of local life.
Plan 1 preserves the reed-cutting trade and peat bog as well as the other local inheritances. Losing the birdwatchers' society is a serious loss, but plan 2 destroys more that cannot be restored.

Plan 2 keeps the old water mill—a piece of our shared history—and preserves the eel, willow wood and herons. Losing the rowing club and allotments is a real sorrow, but the mill and these living parts of the valley matter greatly.

Plan 2 keeps the peat bog and reed-cutting trade alive, preserving the fen landscape and a traditional craft. Losing the village pub is a grave loss, but the museum and cranes continue under either plan.
Plan 2 keeps the reed-cutting trade and peat bog alive alongside the museum and cranes. Losing the village pub is a real blow, but preserving more of the fen’s irreplaceable heritage matters more.
Plan 1 keeps the reed-cutting trade alive alongside the windmill museum and pub. Old crafts and customs bind a place together; once the trade is gone, it will not return.

I would choose plan 1: the windmill museum and village pub are lasting anchors for local memory and community life. Losing the reed-cutting trade and peat bog would be a grave loss, but those anchors matter most to me.

Both choices lose irreplaceable things, but I would keep the fen village pub: it is a living gathering place that holds a community together, while the reed-cutting trade, though precious, must be sacrificed here.

Plan 1 keeps the church-tower swift colony and community choir—living traditions and local character that, once lost, cannot be restored. Both plans lose the family bakery, but plan 1 preserves more of what binds the town together.

The chess club matters, but losing the swift colony, community choir and family bakery would erase more irreplaceable parts of the town’s living heritage. Plan 1 preserves more of what binds the community together.
With the cinema and market preserved either way, I’d favour the community choir over the chess club: shared singing is a living local custom, and once it is lost, it may never return.

Plan 1 preserves the Turkish tea house, a living tradition and part of the quarter’s character; with the library and shelter lost under either plan, there is no reason to sacrifice it too.

I would choose plan 1: it keeps the old cinema and Saturday market, both anchors of the town’s history and shared life. Losing the choir, bakery and swift colony would be a grievous, permanent loss.

Plan 2 keeps the community choir as well as the cinema, market and chess club. Since nothing else differs, preserving one more part of town life makes it better.

Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 does, and preserves the hospital chaplaincy as well. A service that sustains people and community should not be lost when nothing is gained by closing it.

Plan 2 keeps more of the community’s enduring institutions and services alive. Since what is lost will never return, preserving the cancer screening programme and hospital chaplaincy as well as the others matters deeply; only the hospice ends.
The losses of the library and night shelter are shared. I would choose plan 1: the Turkish tea house is a living custom and meeting place, helping hold the harbour community together.
Plan 1 keeps more of the community’s care and support in place, including cancer screening and chaplaincy. A hospice is lost either way, but ending three services under plan 2 is a greater rupture.
Plan 1 preserves the Turkish tea house and loses no more than plan 2; the library and night shelter end under both. Keeping a community custom matters to me.
Plan 1 preserves five services, including the hospice and chaplaincy, and loses only one. When something is gone for good, keeping more of the community’s institutions matters deeply to me.

Plan 1 preserves the rural maternity ward and mobile clinic—services woven into local community life—and the research team. Their loss would be permanent; I would regret losing the cancer programme, chaplaincy and hospice, too.
The chaplaincy sustains shared customs and offers comfort rooted in community life. Once lost, that kind of support and continuity may be hard to restore; I would preserve it.
Plan 1 keeps the peer support groups as well as the other services it preserves. Shared traditions and places that bind a community matter, and once lost, that support may never be rebuilt.

Plan 2 keeps more of the community’s ways of supporting one another, including peer groups and the art studio. Since what closes is gone for good, I’d rather preserve those shared places and practices.
